```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
here::i_am("posts/inflation-unemployment/index.qmd")
POST_DIR <- here::here("posts", "inflation-unemployment")
a <- readRDS(file.path(POST_DIR, "results/analysis.rds"))
f <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)
date_label <- function(x) format(x, "%B %Y")
qval <- function(label, variable) a$quarterly[[variable]][a$quarterly$label == label]
point <- function(date, variable) a$monthly[[variable]][a$monthly$date == as.Date(date)]
provenance <- read.csv(file.path(POST_DIR, "data/raw/provenance.csv"))
```

## How much did the labor market weaken?

U.S. inflation fell sharply after its 2022 peak. How much did unemployment rise during that decline, and when? This question relates to the [Phillips curve](https://www.stlouisfed.org/publications/page-one-economics/2021/07/15/inflation-expectations-the-phillips-curve-and-the-feds-dual-mandate), which connects inflation and unemployment but does not establish a fixed policy tradeoff. For workers, an endpoint comparison can conceal whether a weakening labor market accompanied the entire adjustment or only its later part.

I examine 2015 through 2024, using the earlier years as context for the adjustment after 2022. The charts suggest an early period of substantial inflation decline with little unemployment movement, followed by a later rise in unemployment. The size of that rise depends on the starting date.

## Data and calculations

I downloaded BLS series [CPIAUCSL](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CPIAUCSL) and [UNRATE](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/UNRATE) programmatically with R's `download.file()` and FRED's public CSV URLs. The [repository includes acquisition and analysis code, saved data, and replication instructions](https://github.com/yipin-grena/aeds6400-blog/tree/main/posts/inflation-unemployment). Its `--refresh` option downloads updated observations; the default reproduces the saved snapshot.

Both series are seasonally adjusted. Unemployment is the percentage of the civilian labor force unemployed. Inflation is `100 × (CPI this month / CPI twelve months earlier − 1)`. An extra year supplies the initial CPI comparison, leaving `r nrow(a$monthly)` matched months. Falling positive inflation means prices increase more slowly, not that they fall. Using adjusted CPI can produce small differences from annual headline rates calculated with unadjusted CPI.

## When did the two rates turn?

Figure 1 focuses on 2022 through 2024. Its aligned panels show whether inflation's decline began at the same time as unemployment's rise.

```{r}
#| label: fig-timeline
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Monthly rates on a common scale. The dotted line marks the inflation peak; points label that peak, the subsequent unemployment trough, and December 2024."
#| fig-alt: "Inflation peaks in June 2022, while unemployment reaches its subsequent low in April 2023 before rising."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results/figures/timeline.png"))
```

Inflation peaked at `r f(a$peak$inflation)`% in `r date_label(a$peak$date)`, when unemployment was `r f(a$peak$UNRATE)`%. By `r date_label(a$end$date)`, the rates were `r f(a$end$inflation)`% and `r f(a$end$UNRATE)`%. That is a `r f(a$peak$inflation - a$end$inflation)` percentage point inflation decline alongside a `r f(a$end$UNRATE - a$peak$UNRATE)` point unemployment rise.

However, unemployment first fell to `r f(a$trough$UNRATE)`% in `r date_label(a$trough$date)`. Measured from that trough, its increase was `r f(a$end$UNRATE - a$trough$UNRATE)` points. Neither baseline is inherently wrong. The first describes movement since peak inflation; the second measures labor market weakening from the subsequent unemployment low.

## Did similar unemployment mean similar inflation?

Those turning points invite a broader comparison. Figure 2 pairs the rates in each month, with colors and shapes separating calendar periods.

```{r}
#| label: fig-scatter
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Each point represents one month. Calendar groups provide historical context and are not estimated structural breaks."
#| fig-alt: "A scatterplot shows different inflation rates at similar unemployment levels across the three calendar periods."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results/figures/scatter.png"))
```

Unemployment was `r f(point("2019-12-01", "UNRATE"))`% in December 2019 and `r f(point("2022-06-01", "UNRATE"))`% in June 2022, but inflation was `r f(point("2019-12-01", "inflation"))`% and `r f(point("2022-06-01", "inflation"))`%, respectively. Similar unemployment did not imply similar inflation. This cautions against interpreting all the points as one stable relationship. The scatterplot, however, hides time ordering within each group, which the final chart restores.

## How did the adjustment unfold?

Figure 3 connects consecutive quarters. Averaging three monthly rates makes the path readable but hides monthly fluctuations. Downward movement means falling inflation; rightward movement means rising unemployment. The horizontal axis is narrower than Figure 2's, so visual distances are not directly comparable.

```{r}
#| label: fig-path
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Arrows follow consecutive quarters. Quarterly inflation is the mean of monthly annual inflation rates, not an annualized quarterly growth rate."
#| fig-alt: "A quarterly path shows substantial initial inflation declines with little unemployment movement, followed by rising unemployment and smaller further inflation declines."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results/figures/path.png"))
```

I use 2023 Q2 as a descriptive comparison point because it contains the monthly unemployment trough. From 2022 Q2 to 2023 Q2, inflation fell from `r f(qval("2022 Q2", "inflation"))`% to `r f(qval("2023 Q2", "inflation"))`%, while unemployment moved from `r f(qval("2022 Q2", "unemployment"))`% to `r f(qval("2023 Q2", "unemployment"))`%. By 2024 Q4, unemployment was `r f(qval("2024 Q4", "unemployment"))`% and inflation was `r f(qval("2024 Q4", "inflation"))`%, a further inflation decline of `r f(qval("2023 Q2", "inflation") - qval("2024 Q4", "inflation"))` points. Differences use unrounded values, so subtracting displayed rates can give a different rounded result.

Using 2023 Q1 or Q3 instead preserves the broad pattern. Across these three cutoffs, early unemployment changes range from `r f(min(a$sensitivity$early_unemployment_change))` to `r f(max(a$sensitivity$early_unemployment_change))` percentage points, while later increases range from `r f(min(a$sensitivity$later_unemployment_change))` to `r f(max(a$sensitivity$later_unemployment_change))` points. The [saved sensitivity table](https://github.com/yipin-grena/aeds6400-blog/blob/main/posts/inflation-unemployment/results/tables/cutoff_sensitivity.csv) reports both variables. This is a descriptive distinction, not proof of a structural break.

## Takeaway and limits

Much of the inflation decline preceded the clearer rise in unemployment. Recognizing that sequence avoids both overstating an immediate tradeoff and overlooking later labor market weakening. The unemployment increase is also larger when measured from its trough rather than from peak inflation.

These charts cannot identify a policy's causal effect. Supply conditions, demand, expectations, and policy can all affect the relationship. National averages also conceal differences across workers and households. The finding describes this episode, not a universal rule about the cost of reducing inflation.

**Data and replication.** BLS via FRED, downloaded `r substr(provenance$retrieved_utc[1], 1, 10)`. Observations reflect the saved download vintage, not information available in real time during the episode.
